ideas.hypothesis: Urban wages and output grow superlinearly with city population, and much of that scaling comes from city average years of schooling. Once average schooling is controlled for, the population scaling exponent falls toward one.
ideas.test: Use Chinese prefecture-level city data (census aggregates plus household survey earnings). Estimate log total wage bill or GDP on log population with and without city average years of schooling, instrumenting schooling with historical higher-education institutions.
ideas.disconfirming: The scaling exponent hardly changes when average schooling is added, or average schooling has no independent effect.

ideas.hypothesis: Regional clusters that run continuing vocational training expand the supply of mid-skilled workers, so skill premia grow more slowly in those regions. If skill premia are mainly set by technology, clusters should instead raise them.
ideas.test: Run a difference-in-differences on formal cluster formation in Romanian (or EU NUTS-2) regions, using regional wage-by-education data from labour force surveys and continuing-training participation rates.
ideas.disconfirming: Skill premia do not change, or rise, in cluster regions relative to comparable non-cluster regions.

ideas.hypothesis: Lifetime-income estimates of the human capital stock are so sensitive to the assumed discount rate and earnings growth that plausible parameter ranges change the estimated stock by more than a factor of two. That range is larger than many cross-country differences used in development accounting.
ideas.test: Recompute Russia's lifetime-income human capital stock over a grid of discount rates (2-8%) and real earnings growth rates (1-5.2%), bootstrapping the survey earnings profiles. Compare the resulting range with the cross-country dispersion of stock-per-worker estimates.
ideas.disconfirming: Estimates vary by much less than cross-country differences across plausible parameter values.

ideas.hypothesis: Managers who invest in general, transferable human capital through lifelong learning (e.g., executive education) entrench themselves less, because their human capital depends less on the specific firm.
ideas.test: Use a panel of Chinese listed firms with hand-collected CEO executive-education histories. Regress entrenchment proxies (anti-takeover provisions, abnormal tenure, low turnover-performance sensitivity) on executive education, with firm and year fixed effects.
ideas.disconfirming: Executive education is unrelated to entrenchment, or managers with more general training entrench more.

ideas.hypothesis: Education pays off in the marriage market (spouse's education and earnings, bargaining power within the household) beyond own earnings. A capability-based valuation of education is therefore larger than an earnings-only valuation, especially for women.
ideas.test: Use household survey data with spouse characteristics and household decision-making modules. Estimate the returns to own schooling in spouse earnings and in decision-making power, alongside the standard own-earnings return.
ideas.disconfirming: Schooling shows no return in spouse quality or household decision power once own earnings are controlled for.

ideas.hypothesis: Careers are more bounded for older workers: prior occupational history matters more for whether they are shortlisted, so past mobility helps young candidates but hurts older ones.
ideas.test: Run a correspondence audit or use agency placement records in which candidate age and prior job-change history vary. Fit a logit of shortlisting on mobility x age group.
ideas.disconfirming: The effect of prior mobility on shortlisting is the same for older and younger candidates.

ideas.hypothesis: Building region- and sex-specific mortality rates into lifetime-income estimation substantially lowers Russia's measured human capital stock, especially for men, and changes regional rankings.
ideas.test: Combine Russian regional life tables with earnings survey profiles. Compute lifetime-income stocks with and without survival probabilities, and compare levels and rank correlations across regions.
ideas.disconfirming: Adding mortality changes the stock by less than about 5% and leaves regional rankings essentially unchanged.

ideas.hypothesis: A farm household's grain yield rises with the average schooling of other farmers in its village, beyond the effect of its own schooling, showing a local external effect of education in agriculture.
ideas.test: Use a Chinese rural household panel with plot-level grain yields. Regress yield on own schooling and leave-one-out village average schooling, with household and year fixed effects and input controls.
ideas.disconfirming: Neighbours' average schooling has no effect on yields once own schooling and inputs are controlled for.

ideas.hypothesis: The skill premium was higher in western China than on the coast because skilled labour was scarce, and the human capital investment under the Western Development strategy narrowed this gap after 2000.
ideas.test: Estimate region-specific Mincer earnings regressions from census microdata samples for 1990, 2000, 2005 and 2010, with a difference-in-differences comparison of western and coastal provinces before and after 2000.
ideas.disconfirming: The western skill premium is not higher at baseline, or it does not narrow relative to the coast after 2000.

ideas.hypothesis: The weak causal link between education spending and growth partly reflects measurement error in education data, which is larger in less developed countries. Using better-measured schooling series strengthens the estimated link most at low development levels.
ideas.test: Re-estimate the Granger-causality and panel growth regressions using two alternative cross-country schooling datasets. Compute reliability ratios by income group and apply errors-in-variables corrections.
ideas.disconfirming: Corrected estimates are no larger, or the correction is no bigger for low-development countries.

ideas.hypothesis: In line with Becker's neutrality assumption rather than Malthusian diminishing returns, faster-growing city populations come with larger human capital spillovers, so the earnings return to city average schooling rises with population growth.
ideas.test: Using Chinese individual earnings surveys merged with city data, interact city average schooling with city population growth in Mincer regressions with individual controls and city fixed effects.
ideas.disconfirming: The interaction is negative or zero, meaning spillovers do not grow, or shrink, with population growth.

ideas.hypothesis: Firms provide more general skills training where training investments are better protected (enforceable training-repayment or non-compete clauses), because they can capture more of the return.
ideas.test: Combine cross-jurisdiction variation in how enforceable non-compete or repayment clauses are (US states or EU countries) with establishment-level training surveys. Estimate training incidence and hours on an enforceability index.
ideas.disconfirming: Training provision does not differ with how well training investments are protected.

ideas.hypothesis: Institutional innovations that relax household-registration (hukou) restrictions on school access reduce educational inequality between migrant and local children in the cities that adopt them.
ideas.test: Run a staggered difference-in-differences on city-level reform dates, using school enrollment, progression to high school and test scores of migrant versus local children from household panel data.
ideas.disconfirming: The migrant-local education gap does not narrow after reforms relative to non-reforming cities.

ideas.hypothesis: The Southern dilemma (education gains without growth) arises because educated young southerners migrate north. Regions with higher graduate out-migration get a smaller growth payoff from rising education.
ideas.test: Use an Italian regional panel (1995-2019) of graduate shares, interregional graduate migration flows and per-capita GDP growth. Regress growth on education interacted with net graduate out-migration.
ideas.disconfirming: Graduate out-migration does not moderate the education-growth relation in southern regions.

ideas.hypothesis: Returns to schooling are lower in Belarus than in Russia because state-dominated wage setting compresses pay, with non-material motivational factors partly standing in for wage incentives.
ideas.test: Estimate comparable Mincer equations from Belarusian household budget survey microdata and Russian longitudinal survey data for the same years, with harmonized schooling and experience variables.
ideas.disconfirming: Returns to schooling in Belarus are equal to or higher than in Russia.

ideas.hypothesis: When plants install newer-vintage capital, older workers' employment falls unless the investment comes with recurrent training. Training moderates the displacement because it offsets the depreciation of older workers' skills.
ideas.test: Run an event study around large equipment-investment spikes in linked employer-employee data, comparing separation rates of workers aged 55 and over with younger workers, split by whether the plant also expanded training.
ideas.disconfirming: Older workers' separations do not rise after vintage upgrades, or training makes no difference.

ideas.hypothesis: Raising the statutory pension age lengthens the payoff horizon for training, so workers aged 50-60 participate more in training afterwards.
ideas.test: Run a cohort difference-in-differences using pension-age reforms (e.g., Japan or Germany), comparing training participation of affected and unaffected birth cohorts in labour force survey data.
ideas.disconfirming: Affected cohorts' training participation does not rise relative to unaffected cohorts.

ideas.hypothesis: Counties that receive more agricultural technologists from planting research institutes see higher grain yields after a lag, through technology transfer to farmers.
ideas.test: Use a Chinese county or provincial panel of extension and research staff assignments and grain yields. Estimate distributed-lag fixed-effects models and panel Granger tests.
ideas.disconfirming: Technologist inflows do not predict yield increases at any lag.

ideas.hypothesis: Industry wage premiums linked to average industry human capital (external effects) are larger in high-trust regions, because trust eases knowledge sharing among workers.
ideas.test: Apply the two-stage approach (Mincer wage equation, then industry-region wage premiums regressed on average schooling) to a household survey, interacting average schooling with regional generalized trust from values surveys.
ideas.disconfirming: Trust does not moderate the link between average human capital and wage premiums.

ideas.hypothesis: As the overlapping-generations model predicts, education policies that sharply raise human capital investment (compulsory schooling extensions) are followed by lower returns to physical capital, as household resources move away from material capital.
ideas.test: Build a cross-country panel with dates of compulsory schooling reforms and returns to physical capital from national accounts. Run event-study regressions over the following 10-20 years.
ideas.disconfirming: Returns to capital rise or stay the same after schooling expansions.

ideas.hypothesis: University expansion (e.g., China after 1999) increased educational assortative mating and raised the marriage-market return to a degree, especially for women.
ideas.test: Use census couple-level microdata to compare spouse education and income matching for birth cohorts just before and after the expansion, with a cohort regression-discontinuity design.
ideas.disconfirming: No change in assortative mating or marriage-market returns to a degree across the expansion cohorts.

ideas.hypothesis: Players from clubs with integrated education programmes have higher post-retirement career mobility and earnings, which offsets the negative human capital accumulation of an athletic career.
ideas.test: Run a tracer survey of retired professional footballers in China, comparing occupational transitions and earnings of players from clubs with and without dual-education programmes and controlling for playing level.
ideas.disconfirming: Post-career mobility and earnings do not differ by exposure to club education programmes.

ideas.hypothesis: Chinese prefecture-level cities with higher average years of schooling attract more foreign investment, especially in skill-intensive industries.
ideas.test: Use a city panel of foreign-invested enterprise entry by industry skill intensity, regressed on lagged average schooling and instrumented with historical university presence.
ideas.disconfirming: Average schooling does not predict foreign investment entry, including in skill-intensive industries.

ideas.hypothesis: Returns to skills in China are higher in the tertiary sector than in manufacturing, and they rise as the local service-sector share grows.
ideas.test: Estimate sector-specific Mincer and skill-test earnings regressions from Chinese household survey microdata, interacting skills with the city service-sector employment share.
ideas.disconfirming: Returns to skills in services are equal to or lower than in manufacturing and do not rise with service share.

ideas.hypothesis: Capability-based measures of what people can do and be with their education reveal a threshold below which extra schooling adds little to wellbeing or income (an education poverty trap), which linear earnings returns miss.
ideas.test: Use household surveys with capability indicators (health, agency, social participation) and earnings. Estimate nonparametric or threshold regressions of outcomes on years of schooling.
ideas.disconfirming: Returns are linear or concave, with no low-schooling threshold, on both capability and earnings outcomes.

ideas.hypothesis: In Belarus, compressed wage distributions inside firms weaken employees' motivation to upgrade skills, so firms with more internal wage dispersion have higher training uptake and productivity.
ideas.test: Run a matched firm-employee survey in Belarusian enterprises measuring internal wage dispersion, motivation scales and training participation, and regress training on wage dispersion with industry controls.
ideas.disconfirming: Wage dispersion is unrelated or negatively related to motivation and training uptake.

ideas.hypothesis: Adding health capital (via health-adjusted life expectancy) to human capital stock estimates changes the human-to-physical capital ratio and improves how well the stock explains output in growth accounting.
ideas.test: For Russian regions, compute lifetime-income human capital stocks with and without a health adjustment. Compare the fit of regional output regressions on each stock measure using information criteria.
ideas.disconfirming: The health-adjusted stock does not improve explanatory power over the unadjusted stock.

ideas.hypothesis: Within industrial clusters, workplace-based hands-on continuing vocational training produces larger firm productivity gains than classroom-based training of equal hours.
ideas.test: Survey firms in the North-West Romanian clusters on training format and hours, linked to balance-sheet productivity. Estimate productivity changes by training type with firm fixed effects.
ideas.disconfirming: Productivity gains do not differ by training format.

ideas.hypothesis: Minimum wage increases reduce employer-funded lifelong learning for low-wage older workers, because employers can no longer pass training costs on as lower wages.
ideas.test: Run a difference-in-differences on regional minimum wage increases using labour force survey training modules, focusing on workers aged 50 and over earning near the minimum compared with higher earners.
ideas.disconfirming: Training of affected low-wage older workers does not fall, or rises, after minimum wage increases.

ideas.hypothesis: The overlapping-generations inverse relation between human capital investment and the return on physical capital weakens in economies with high international capital mobility, because world interest rates pin down domestic capital returns.
ideas.test: Use a cross-country panel regressing returns to physical capital on public education spending, interacted with a capital-account openness index, with country and year fixed effects.
ideas.disconfirming: The negative relation is equally strong in high- and low-capital-mobility economies.
